query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, an optimum Al/Cr ratio governs phase stability by maximizing lattice distortion and promoting the preferential formation of protective, ordered alumina/chromia at the grain boundaries that both suppresses deleterious intermetallic precipitation and lowers defect mobility. This stable disordered FCC matrix, in turn, is responsible for maintaining high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy exhibiting a disordered (FCC) single-phase microstructure in the as-cast state.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the Al/Cr atomic ratio (while keeping Co, Fe, and Ni constant) during alloy synthesis, comparing alloys having lower, optimal, and higher Al/Cr ratios under identical processing conditions.
generation.conditions: All alloys will be synthesized via the same melting and cooling process (e.g., arc melting or directed energy deposition) to ensure identical thermal histories. Subsequent evaluations include high-temperature mechanical tests with oxidation exposure, controlled ion irradiation experiments, and cryogenic tensile tests, with each test performed under the same environmental and loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The maintenance of a stable FCC matrix and the development of protective, ordered α-Al2O3/Cr2O3 scales at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: An optimal amount of Al (relative to Cr) increases lattice distortion and triggers the selective formation of protective alumina/chromia layers. This mechanism suppresses the nucleation of embrittling intermetallic phases and retards defect mobility (thereby enhancing radiation tolerance), while also lowering stacking fault energy sufficiently to activate deformation twinning, which improves cryogenic toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy, the alloy with the optimum Al/Cr ratio is predicted to exhibit: (i) a retained single-phase FCC structure with minimal secondary phase precipitates, (ii) formation of a denser, more uniform protective oxide scale during high-temperature exposure, (iii) less radiation-induced hardening (indicative of better defect management), and (iv) improved cryogenic fracture toughness (via enhanced twinning).
generation.baseline: The standard equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA with its default (balanced) Al/Cr ratio.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys with near-equiatomic proportions of Co, Fe, and Ni, and with modest variations in the Al/Cr ratio that still allow formation of an FCC solid solution. It does not extend to alloy systems where large compositional shifts produce non-FCC phases.
generation.uncertainty: Although the directional effects are supported by prior oxidation and phase analysis studies, the exact optimal Al/Cr ratio and the quantitative magnitude of improvements in each property (high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness) remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs with systematically varied Al/Cr ratios (e.g., below, at, and above the predicted optimum) using identical processing conditions. Characterize the phase structure (via XRD and EBSD) and assess the oxide scale formation (via SEM/EDS) after high-temperature exposure. Perform mechanical testing at high temperature, subject samples to controlled irradiation (monitoring hardness changes and defect characteristics), and conduct cryogenic tensile tests to evaluate fracture toughness.
measurements: Phase composition and microstructure (FCC vs. secondary phases)
Oxide scale composition, uniformity, and thickness
Mechanical properties: tensile strength and ductility at high and cryogenic temperatures
Radiation-induced changes in hardness or defect structure
Grain boundary features and the presence of deformation twins
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no systematic correlation is observed between the Al/Cr ratio and the retention of a stable FCC phase with protective oxide formation, or if variations in the Al/Cr ratio do not translate into enhanced high-temperature strength, improved radiation tolerance, and better cryogenic toughness compared to the baseline alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As reported by Listyawan et al. [], our model also demonstrates a considerable presence of Fe3O4 and Fe2O3 in the oxide scale due to the high diffusion coefficient of Fe at low temperatures []. A careful observation of the time-dependent concentration change plots for varying Al to Cr ratios shows an interesting difference between Al and Cr oxides with the rest of the oxides. The fluctuation of the concentration of thermodynamically unstable oxide (Fe, Co, and Ni oxides) is higher than thermodynamically stable oxides (Al and Cr oxides), making the lines of Figure 5d–f appear thicker than Figure 5b,c. Similar observations can be made for all the oxide concentration plots, as well. As Fe, Co, and Ni oxides are thermodynamically unstable, the formation and dissociation occur more frequently in these oxides as compared to Al and Cr oxides.
